To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of a hierarchical model for the analysis of a clinical trial of an agent for pain relief allows the investigator to address the questions of proof of efficacy and of dosage recommendation and (2) the use of such a model allows the investigator to make use of information about the mechanism of action of the agent and about the nature of the pain relief process to improve the accuracy of the dosage recommendations.
the proposed analysis of analgesic trial results can address both the question of proof of efficacy and the question of optimal dosing.
a subject-specific pain-relieved model can be used to estimate the probability of remedication, given pain relief and subject-specific random effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of nonrandomly censored ordered categorical longitudinal data.

the analysis of data from clinical trials in which the primary outcome is a time-varying, ordered categorical response, such as pain relief scores, and the response process is subject to right censoring, such as remedication.
the development of statistical methodology that can be applied in the context of clinical trials of drugs for the treatment of pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a given dose of drug relieves pain, on average, to some extent, for some patients, and that the dose should be used in further trials, or recommended for typical patients, if and only if the extrapolation is credible.
the data support the use of the drug for pain relief and that the drug is effective for a typical subject in a range of dosing regimens.
, on the basis of this trial, the drug ketoralac is a pain reliever, and a typical patient would benefit most by taking 30 mg at 4 hr intervals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the proposed hierarchical model provides a more complete and credible analysis of the study data than does a marginal model, and that the proposed analysis can be used to address the two questions of interest.
the proposed analysis of analgesic trial results provides a better answer to the dosing-recommendation question than the analysis suggested by the authors of the paper under discussion.
we propose to use the hierarchical model as a tool to extrapolate the dosing question to the population of interest, and that we use a semimechanistically motivated model to do this.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a subject-specific model for the distributional structure of pain relief data, conditional on individual effects, is an effective approach to the analysis of such data.
the analysis of a trial based on a hierarchical model can provide a more comprehensive analysis of a trial than an analysis based on a marginal model.

a model-based analysis of the data from analgesic trials can provide a more comprehensive and credible answer to the questions that are of interest to clinicians than can be obtained from an analysis based on marginal models of human pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.
